original_question: Let the width of a group(respectively, a monoid) H with respect to a generating set X mean the supremum over h ∈ H of the least length of a group word(respectively, a monoid word) in elements of X expressing h. A group(or monoid) is said to have finite width if its width with respect to every generating set is finite. (A common finite bound for these widths is not required.) Do there exist groups G having finite width as groups, but not as monoids? This is Question 9 in(G. M. Bergman, Bull. London Math. Soc., 38(2006), 429–440).
target_in_paper: Problem 21.16 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)" of The Kourovka Notebook.
correct_elements: Your draft is already extremely close to the paper: it reproduces the official definition of width with respect to a generating set, includes the paper's parenthetical clarification that no common bound over all generating sets is required, and asks the same existence question stated in Problem 21.16.
missing_details: Make explicit that in the group case, X ranges over subsets that generate G as a group, while in the monoid case, X ranges over subsets that generate G as a monoid.
Spell out that a group word may use letters from X and their inverses, whereas a monoid word uses only letters from X (no inverses).
State explicitly that the length is the number of letters in the shortest such word.
Unpack "not as monoids" as: there exists some monoid generating set Y for G for which no finite bound works for the lengths of positive words representing all elements of G.
If one wants the formulation to be fully stand-alone, note that the width is a supremum in N union {infinity}.
refined_question: Does there exist a group G such that, for every subset X ⊆ G that generates G as a group, there is a finite integer n_X with the property that every g ∈ G can be expressed as a word of length at most n_X in the alphabet X ∪ X^{-1}, but for some subset Y ⊆ G that generates G as a monoid, the positive-word lengths with respect to Y are unbounded; equivalently, for every m ∈ N there exists g ∈ G that cannot be written as a product of at most m elements of Y?
justification: Problem 21.16 is the nearest official formulation in arXiv:1401.0300, and your draft is essentially a verbatim transcription of that problem. Although 21.16 points back to Bergman's 2006 Question 9, the Kourovka formulation isolates only the existence question about separating finite width in the group sense from finite width in the monoid sense, so the refined version should preserve exactly that narrower focus rather than expand to the broader two-part original question. The only real improvements needed are to make the quantifiers over generating sets and the failure of the monoid version completely explicit.
